skills.name: aria-attributes
skills.title: ARIA Attributes
skills.description: Use when asked to add or review ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes — roles, states, and properties for dynamic/interactive elements — as a supplement to semantic HTML, not a replacement for it, and grounded in web-content-accessibility-guidelines' operable/perceivable criteria.

skills.name: cross-cultural-communication
skills.title: Cross Cultural Communication
skills.description: Use when asked to communicate effectively across cultural backgrounds — cultural awareness, language differences, nonverbal communication, direct/indirect and high/low-context styles, sensitivity and adaptation — as a communication discipline, distinct from inclusive-language's specific wording focus.

skills.name: digital-inclusion
skills.title: Digital Inclusion
skills.description: Use when asked about ensuring all individuals and communities can access and effectively use digital technologies — connectivity, digital skills/literacy, accessibility, culturally appropriate content, digital citizenship and safety — as the broad societal umbrella that accessibility-testing and web-content-accessibility-guidelines address one dimension of.

skills.name: keyboard-shortcut
skills.title: Keyboard Shortcut
skills.description: Use when asked to design or document keyboard shortcuts (hotkeys) — accelerating workflow, accessibility for mobility-impaired users, consistency/standardization, customization — for a software application or operating system.

skills.name: screen-reader
skills.title: Screen Reader
skills.description: Use when asked about how screen readers work and how to design/build for them — audio representation of content, semantic markup and alt text, navigation mechanisms, structural/context cues — as the underlying assistive technology screen-reader-testing verifies against.

skills.name: web-content-accessibility-guidelines
skills.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
skills.description: Use when asked about WCAG specifically — the perceivable/operable/understandable/robust (POUR) principles and A/AA/AAA conformance levels — as the formal standard accessibility-testing and screen-reader-testing verify compliance against.

skills.name: demand-analysis
skills.title: Demand Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to run or explain a demand analysis — estimating and understanding customer demand for a product or service (market size, price sensitivity, demand drivers) — as the market-feasibility input to a broader feasibility-analysis or business case.

skills.name: feasibility-analysis
skills.title: Feasibility Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to run or explain a feasibility analysis — assessing whether a proposed project, product, or venture is practically achievable across technical, financial, operational, legal, and market dimensions — before committing significant resources to it.

skills.name: five-forces-analysis
skills.title: Five Forces Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to run or explain a Porter's Five Forces analysis — assessing industry competitiveness via rivalry, supplier/buyer power, and threats of new entrants/substitutes — as an industry-structure framework complementary to swot-analysis and pestle-analysis.

skills.name: pestle-analysis
skills.title: PESTLE Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to run or explain a PESTLE (or PEST) analysis — the macro-environmental factors framework for strategic planning — sourced from Wikipedia's PEST analysis article, including its PESTEL/STEEPLE variants and known limitations.

skills.name: stakeholder-analysis
skills.title: Stakeholder Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to run or explain a stakeholder analysis — identifying stakeholders and mapping their interest and influence (a power/interest grid) to plan engagement — as the analytical step that typically precedes formalizing responsibilities in a responsibility-assignment-matrix.

skills.name: swot-analysis
skills.title: SWOT Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to run or explain a SWOT analysis — Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats — the internal-vs-external strategic planning framework, sourced from Wikipedia's SWOT analysis article, including its history and known limitations.

skills.name: angel-investor
skills.title: Angel Investor
skills.description: Use when asked about angel investors — high-net-worth individuals investing their own money in early-stage startups, typically before venture-capital involvement — as a distinct, usually smaller and more personally-involved funding source.

skills.name: board-deck
skills.title: Board Deck
skills.description: Use when asked to build or review a board deck — a presentation for a company's board of directors summarizing performance, risks, and decisions needed — distinct from an [[investor-update]], which is a lighter, more frequent written update rather than a governance-meeting presentation.

skills.name: branding
skills.title: Branding
skills.description: Use when asked to develop or apply a brand — brand identity, brand strategy, brand guidelines, consistency across touchpoints — as distinct from a single campaign or the broader marketing-manager function, which branding underlies and constrains.

skills.name: business-development
skills.title: Business Development
skills.description: Use when asked about business development — market analysis, strategic partnerships, lead generation, relationship management, and expansion activities that grow a company's market position — as the broader function that joint-venture, spinoff, and spinout structures often serve.

skills.name: business-model-canvas
skills.title: Business Model Canvas
skills.description: Use when asked to build or explain a Business Model Canvas — a one-page, nine-block visual template covering value proposition, customer segments, channels, revenue, cost structure, and more — as a structured way to design or communicate a business model before or alongside a full business plan.

skills.name: business-model-innovation
skills.title: Business Model Innovation
skills.description: Use when asked about business model innovation — deliberately rethinking how a company creates, delivers, and captures value (not just its products) — as distinct from product innovation, and often expressed using the business-model-canvas as a working tool.

skills.name: communications-manager
skills.title: Communications Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the internal/organizational communications function — leadership messaging, change communications, or an internal communications plan — as distinct from public relations (see public-relations-manager), which targets external audiences, and general team communication norms (see ways-of-working).

skills.name: crisis-communication-plan
skills.title: Crisis Communication Plan
skills.description: Use when asked to write a crisis communication plan — how an organization communicates externally, to media, customers, or the public, during a crisis — as distinct from an [[incident-response-plan]], which covers the internal operational or technical response rather than the external-facing message.

skills.name: finance-manager
skills.title: Finance Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the finance management function — budgeting/forecasting, financial statements (P&L, balance sheet, cash flow), unit economics, or a business case's financial justification — as an organizational function, not as personal financial or investment advice.

skills.name: information-manager
skills.title: Information Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the information management function — information governance, data classification/retention, records management, or information security policy at the organizational level — as distinct from a technical database or security-tooling skill, which this function relies on but doesn't itself specify.

skills.name: investor-update
skills.title: Investor Update
skills.description: Use when asked to write a regular investor update — a concise, often-monthly written update on company progress sent to investors — distinct from a full [[board-deck]], which is prepared for a formal governance meeting rather than a lighter, more frequent written note.

skills.name: joint-venture
skills.title: Joint Venture
skills.description: Use when asked about a joint venture (JV) — two or more independent entities forming a new, separate entity to pursue a shared business objective — as distinct from a general strategic partnership, and from spinoff/spinout, which separate a piece of one company rather than combine two.

skills.name: legal-manager
skills.title: Legal Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the in-house legal/general counsel function — contract review, corporate compliance, IP protection, or risk/liability management — as an organizational function, not as a substitute for actual legal advice from a qualified lawyer for a specific real situation or jurisdiction.

skills.name: market-expansion
skills.title: Market Expansion
skills.description: Use when asked about market expansion — growing a business by entering new geographic markets or customer segments with an existing offering — as distinct from product-line-extension, which grows by adding new offerings to an existing market.

skills.name: marketing-manager
skills.title: Marketing Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the marketing management function — brand positioning, the marketing mix, campaign planning, or marketing metrics (CAC, LTV, funnel conversion) — as distinct from sales management (see sales-manager) or public relations (see public-relations-manager), which marketing coordinates closely with but is not the same function as.

skills.name: operations-manager
skills.title: Operations Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the operations management function — process design/improvement, capacity planning, SLAs and service quality, or vendor/supplier management — as distinct from project management (see project-management), which manages bounded work rather than ongoing operational delivery.

skills.name: product-line-extension
skills.title: Product Line Extension
skills.description: Use when asked about product line extension — growing a business by adding new products/variants for an existing customer base — as distinct from market-expansion, which grows by reaching new markets with an existing offering.

skills.name: public-relations-manager
skills.title: Public Relations Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the public relations (PR) function — media relations, a press release, crisis/reputation management, or stakeholder communications strategy — as distinct from marketing (see marketing-manager) or internal communications (see communications-manager), which PR coordinates closely with but is not the same function as.

skills.name: sales-manager
skills.title: Sales Manager
skills.description: Use when asked about the sales management function — pipeline/funnel management, sales methodologies (BANT, MEDDIC, SPIN), quota/forecast management, or CRM discipline — as distinct from marketing (see marketing-manager), which generates and qualifies demand that sales then converts.

skills.name: spinoff
skills.title: Spinoff
skills.description: Use when asked about a corporate spinoff — a parent company creating a new independent company by selling or distributing some of its assets or operations — as distinct from spinout (employee-initiated) and joint-venture (combining rather than separating entities).

skills.name: spinout
skills.title: Spinout
skills.description: Use when asked about a spinout (employee spinout) — employees taking a technology or product and developing it into a new independent company — as distinct from spinoff (parent-initiated corporate restructuring).

skills.name: venture-capital
skills.title: Venture Capital
skills.description: Use when asked about venture capital (VC) — how VC funding works, funding stages, what VCs look for, and the trade-offs of taking VC money — as a specific, larger-scale, professionally managed funding source distinct from angel-investor funding.

skills.name: big-hairy-audacious-goal
skills.title: Big Hairy Audacious Goal
skills.description: Use when asked to write a BHAG (Big Hairy Audacious Goal) — a long-horizon, ambitious statement of ultimate organizational purpose — as distinct from a nearer-term, directly trackable North Star metric (see north-star) that operationalizes progress toward it.

skills.name: critical-success-factors
skills.title: Critical Success Factors
skills.description: Use when asked to identify Critical Success Factors (CSFs) — the few essential areas an organization must excel at to achieve its mission — as the qualitative, area-of-focus counterpart to key-performance-indicators's quantitative metrics, and a direct input to strategic-balanced-scorecard.

skills.name: emergent-task-planning
skills.title: Emergent Task Planning
skills.description: Use when asked to apply Emergent Task Planning (ETP) — Francis Seah's just-in-time, flexible-goal productivity framework for unpredictable environments — as distinct from a fixed, upfront-planned approach like a yearly-planning-meeting's annual cycle or a rigid work-breakdown-structure.

skills.name: guide-star
skills.title: Guide Star
skills.description: Use when asked about a "guiding star" objective — the single overarching goal orienting a team or organization's decisions — the same underlying concept as a North Star metric (see north-star), under an alternate name some teams and frameworks use.

skills.name: key-performance-indicators
skills.title: Key Performance Indicators
skills.description: Use when asked to define, choose, or improve a Key Performance Indicator (KPI) — leading vs lagging indicators, measure vs metric, or how to check whether a proposed KPI is actually good — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/key-performance-indicator, as distinct from OKRs (see objectives-and-key-results).

skills.name: key-risk-indicators
skills.title: Key Risk Indicators
skills.description: Use when asked to define or choose a Key Risk Indicator (KRI) — an early-warning metric for organizational risk — as the risk-focused counterpart to key-performance-indicators's performance-focused metrics, typically used together for a full view of health.

skills.name: maturity-models
skills.title: Maturity Models
skills.description: Use when asked to design, apply, or explain a maturity model — level naming conventions, top-down vs bottom-up construction, or well-known examples (CMMI, DevOps, Agile maturity models) — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/maturity-models, including documented rebuttals.

skills.name: north-star
skills.title: North Star
skills.description: Use when asked to define a North Star metric or objective — the single overarching goal guiding a company's strategy and decisions — as distinct from a Big Hairy Audacious Goal (see big-hairy-audacious-goal), which is longer-horizon and more aspirational than a trackable North Star metric.

skills.name: objectives-and-key-results
skills.title: Objectives and Key Results
skills.description: Use when asked to write OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) — an inspirational, team-actionable objective paired with measurable key results — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/objectives-and-key-results, including known real-world pros/cons, as distinct from KPIs alone (see key-performance-indicators).

skills.name: pitch-deck
skills.title: Pitch Deck
skills.description: Use when asked to write, structure, or critique a startup pitch deck — fundraising slideshow content, common templates, or investor-advice frameworks (market-first, asymmetric bets, aggregation theory) — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/pitch-deck.

skills.name: plan-do-check-act
skills.title: Plan Do Check Act
skills.description: Use when asked to explain or apply the PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) improvement cycle, its PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) variant, or how it compares to other iterative-improvement cycles (OODA, DMAIC) — sourced from Wikipedia's PDCA article.

skills.name: smart-criteria
skills.title: SMART Criteria
skills.description: Use when asked to write or check a goal/objective/task against SMART criteria (Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Relatable, Timely) or its SMARTER/FAST extensions — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/smart-criteria, as a quality check that pairs with OKRs (see objectives-and-key-results) and KPIs (see key-performance-indicators).

skills.name: strategic-balanced-scorecard
skills.title: Strategic Balanced Scorecard
skills.description: Use when asked to build a strategic balanced scorecard — a destination statement across financial/external/internal/learning perspectives, connected to OKRs, KPIs, and CSFs — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/strategic-balanced-scorecard, as distinct from the plain OKR or KPI frameworks it connects.

skills.name: total-project-control
skills.title: Total Project Control
skills.description: Use when asked to explain or apply Total Project Control (TPC) — Stephen Devaux's ROI-focused project-management method, critical path drag, DIPP, and Value Breakdown Structure — sourced from Wikipedia's Total project control article, as distinct from the plain Critical Path Method (see critical-path).

skills.name: vision-mission-values
skills.title: Vision Mission Values
skills.description: Use when asked to write a vision statement, mission statement, or set of organizational values — the three foundational components of a company's strategic plan — as distinct from a North Star metric (see north-star) or BHAG (see big-hairy-audacious-goal), which operationalize a vision into something trackable.

skills.name: voice-of-the-customer
skills.title: Voice of the Customer
skills.description: Use when asked to capture and act on customer feedback — VoC channels (surveys, focus groups, support interactions, social media) feeding product decisions — as the customer-facing input that grounds objective-setting (see objectives-and-key-results) and product management (see product-management) in real user need.

skills.name: volatile-uncertain-complex-ambiguous
skills.title: Volatile Uncertain Complex Ambiguous
skills.description: Use when asked to apply the VUCA framework (Volatile, Uncertain, Complex, Ambiguous) to describe or navigate a turbulent business environment — as a diagnostic lens for choosing an appropriate response, distinct from applying any one specific strategic framework (see swot-analysis, pestle-analysis) without first identifying which VUCA dimension is actually at play.

skills.name: adkar
skills.title: ADKAR
skills.description: Use when asked to plan organizational change adoption at the individual level — Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement (Prosci's ADKAR model) — as the individual-change-adoption complement to process-improvement methodologies like Kaizen and DMAIC (see kaizen, dmaic), which improve the process itself rather than how people adopt it.

skills.name: critical-to-quality
skills.title: Critical to Quality
skills.description: Use when asked to define Critical to Quality (CTQ) requirements in a Six Sigma context — translating customer expectations into measurable product/service characteristics with performance targets — as distinct from the general SQA catalog (see system-quality-attributes) and feeding directly into a dmaic project's Define/Measure stages.

skills.name: dmaic
skills.title: DMAIC
skills.description: Use when asked to run a Six Sigma DMAIC improvement project — Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control — as a data-driven, project-scoped alternative to Kaizen's continuous, incremental cycle (see kaizen) or PDCA's general iterative loop (see plan-do-check-act).

skills.name: kaizen
skills.title: Kaizen
skills.description: Use when asked to apply Kaizen — continuous, incremental, all-employee process improvement built on the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle (see plan-do-check-act) — as distinct from a project-scoped Six Sigma DMAIC effort (see dmaic), which is heavier-weight and typically team-led rather than everyone-participating.

skills.name: six-sigma
skills.title: Six Sigma
skills.description: Use when asked about the Six Sigma quality-management methodology as a whole — belt-level roles, sigma levels/defects-per-million, and choosing between DMAIC (improving an existing process, see dmaic) or DMADV/DFSS (designing a new one) — as distinct from running the DMAIC cycle itself, which this skill defers to for the step-by-step improvement procedure.

skills.name: vanguard-method
skills.title: Vanguard Method
skills.description: Use when asked to apply the Vanguard Method (John Seddon's systems-thinking approach) to redesign a service organization — studying demand, flow, and capability as an integrated system before changing anything — as distinct from transplanting a manufacturing-derived methodology like six-sigma onto service work, which the method's originator specifically argues against.

skills.name: agile-charter
skills.title: Agile Charter
skills.description: Use when asked to run an agile chartering session — collaboratively defining a project's vision, objectives, and working agreement with a diverse stakeholder group — as distinct from a formal project charter document (see project-charter), which is written and approved rather than co-created in a session.

skills.name: agile-coaching
skills.title: Agile Coaching
skills.description: Use when asked about the agile coach role — facilitating ceremonies, removing impediments, fostering psychological safety, and evolving from hands-on guidance to strategic coaching as a team matures — as distinct from a Scrum Master's more process-focused role or a traditional project manager (see project-management).

skills.name: agile-delivery
skills.title: Agile Delivery
skills.description: Use when asked to run the delivery track of dual-track agile — building, testing, and shipping validated work via a continuous delivery pipeline — as the track that runs alongside, not after, discovery (see agile-discovery), and grounded in continuous delivery's build/test/deploy/release pipeline.

skills.name: agile-discovery
skills.title: Agile Discovery
skills.description: Use when asked to run the discovery track of dual-track agile — validating what to build before building it, via problem identification, user personas, and prototyping — as the track that runs alongside, not before, delivery (see agile-delivery), and feeds product-management's broader discipline.

skills.name: agile-liftoff
skills.title: Agile Liftoff
skills.description: Use when asked to run an agile project liftoff — aligning a team on vision, objectives, stakeholders, and initial plan at project start — as distinct from an agile chartering session's working-agreement focus (see agile-charter) or a formal project charter document (see project-charter).

skills.name: agile-principles
skills.title: Agile Principles
skills.description: Use when asked what the Agile principles are, to check a team practice or process decision against them, or to explain the reasoning behind agile software delivery (as opposed to a specific framework like Scrum or Kanban, which implement these principles rather than being identical to them).

skills.name: agile-reflection
skills.title: Agile Reflection
skills.description: Use when asked to run a team reflection or retrospective in the spirit of the 12th Agile Manifesto principle — regular, honest process examination followed by actual behavior change — as distinct from a futurespective's forward-looking scenario exploration (see futurespective), which looks ahead rather than back.

skills.name: agile-showcase
skills.title: Agile Showcase
skills.description: Use when asked to run an agile showcase (sprint review) — demonstrating working software to stakeholders on a regular cadence — including whether a team should run one at all, mirroring the same with/without tradeoff agile-standup covers for daily standups.

skills.name: agile-standown
skills.title: Agile Standown
skills.description: Use when asked about an agile "stand-down" — an informal end-of-day or end-of-session closing check-in some teams run as the counterpart to a morning standup (see agile-standup). This is a less standardized, less common practice than the standup itself — verify what a specific team actually means by the term before assuming a fixed format.

skills.name: agile-standup
skills.title: Agile Standup
skills.description: Use when asked to run a daily standup (daily scrum) — the three-question format, timeboxing, and common failure modes — including whether a team should even run one at all, as distinct from a broader agile-coaching engagement (see agile-coaching) that would help diagnose that question.

skills.name: disciplined-agile
skills.title: Disciplined Agile
skills.description: Use when asked to choose or tailor a team's "way of working" (WoW) with Disciplined Agile (DA) — a goal-driven toolkit of decision points and options spanning multiple lifecycles, rather than one prescribed process — as distinct from adopting a single fixed framework like scrum, scaled-agile-framework, or large-scale-scrum outright.

skills.name: extreme-programming
skills.title: Extreme Programming
skills.description: Use when asked to apply Extreme Programming (XP) — pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, refactoring, and sustainable pace as the specific engineering practices behind agile delivery — as distinct from scrum's process/role framework, which XP's practices are commonly run inside rather than as a competing alternative.

skills.name: kanban
skills.title: Kanban
skills.description: Use when asked to set up or run a Kanban board — columns, work-in-progress limits, continuous flow — as an alternative to Scrum's fixed sprints (see scrum), suited to continuous-flow work rather than timeboxed iterations.

skills.name: large-scale-scrum
skills.title: Large Scale Scrum
skills.description: Use when asked to scale scrum across many teams with LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum) — one Product Backlog, one Product Owner, and one Sprint shared across all teams, deliberately minimizing added roles and process — as distinct from scaled-agile-framework's more prescriptive, role-heavy approach to the same scaling problem.

skills.name: scaled-agile-framework
skills.title: Scaled Agile Framework
skills.description: Use when asked to scale agile delivery across many teams with SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) — Agile Release Trains, PI Planning, and Portfolio/Large Solution/Essential configurations — as distinct from large-scale-scrum's deliberately minimal alternative for the same scaling problem, and from disciplined-agile's goal-driven toolkit approach rather than a single prescribed structure.

skills.name: scrum
skills.title: Scrum
skills.description: Use when asked to set up or run Scrum — roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team), artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment), and events (sprint planning, daily scrum, review, retrospective) — as a fixed-sprint alternative to Kanban's continuous flow (see kanban).

skills.name: scrum-of-scrums
skills.title: Scrum of Scrums
skills.description: Use when asked to coordinate multiple scrum teams working on one product via a Scrum of Scrums meeting — a lightweight cross-team sync sending one ambassador per team — as distinct from adopting a full scaling framework like large-scale-scrum or scaled-agile-framework, which restructure roles and planning rather than just adding a coordination meeting.

skills.name: scrumban
skills.title: Scrumban
skills.description: Use when asked to run Scrumban — a hybrid blending scrum's planning structure with kanban's continuous-flow board and WIP limits, pulling work on demand rather than committing to a fixed sprint backlog — for a team that needs more structure than pure Kanban but finds Scrum's fixed sprint commitment a poor fit for their work's variability.

skills.name: citation-style-ama
skills.title: Citation Style Ama
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in AMA (American Medical Association) citation style, 11th edition, used in medical journals and the clinical sciences; numbered like [[citation-style-vancouver]], but with superscript numbers and its own manual.

skills.name: citation-style-apa
skills.title: Citation Style Apa
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in APA (American Psychological Association) citation style, 7th edition, used in psychology, education, the social sciences, nursing, and business; author-date like [[citation-style-harvard]], but with a fixed official manual; unlike the numbered [[citation-style-ieee]] and [[citation-style-vancouver]].

skills.name: citation-style-chicago
skills.title: Citation Style Chicago
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in Chicago Manual of Style citation, in both of its systems, used in history, the arts, the humanities (notes-bibliography), and the sciences and social sciences (author-date); a style with two systems, unlike the single-system [[citation-style-apa]] and [[citation-style-mla]].

skills.name: citation-style-harvard
skills.title: Citation Style Harvard
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in Harvard citation style, used in business, the sciences, and the social sciences, especially in the United Kingdom and Australia; author-date like [[citation-style-apa]], but with no single official manual.

skills.name: citation-style-ieee
skills.title: Citation Style Ieee
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) citation style, used in engineering, computer science, and electronics; numbered like [[citation-style-vancouver]], but with initials first and a distinct punctuation pattern.

skills.name: citation-style-mla
skills.title: Citation Style Mla
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in MLA (Modern Language Association) citation style, 9th edition, used in literature, languages, the humanities, and cultural studies; author-page rather than author-date like [[citation-style-apa]], with a Works Cited list rather than numbered references.

skills.name: citation-style-oscola
skills.title: Citation Style Oscola
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in OSCOLA (Oxford Standard for the Citation of Legal Authorities), used in law, especially in the United Kingdom; a footnote-based legal style, unlike the author-date [[citation-style-apa]] and numbered [[citation-style-ieee]].

skills.name: citation-style-vancouver
skills.title: Citation Style Vancouver
skills.description: Use when asked to cite sources, format in-text citations, or build a reference list in Vancouver citation style, used in medicine, nursing, and the biomedical sciences; numbered like [[citation-style-ieee]] and [[citation-style-ama]], with a plain, compact reference format.

skills.name: medical-clinical-supervision
skills.title: Medical Clinical Supervision
skills.description: Use when asked to explain or structure clinical supervision — regular, protected mentorship and oversight of a nurse or junior doctor by a more senior clinician, supporting both development and patient safety — for general educational and structural guidance only, not medical advice; always follow institutional policy and consult a qualified health care professional.

skills.name: medical-nurse-staffing-ratio-planning
skills.title: Medical Nurse Staffing Ratio Planning
skills.description: Use when asked to explain or structure nurse staffing ratio planning — setting staffing levels against patient acuity and workload rather than a flat headcount, to keep care safe and sustainable — for general educational and structural guidance only, not medical advice; always follow institutional policy and consult a qualified health care professional.

skills.name: always-improving
skills.title: Always Improving
skills.description: Use when asked to summarize or apply ideas from popular self-improvement and business books (Grit, Start with Why, The Lean Startup, The Power of Habit, Zero to One, and others) — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/always-improving's curated summary list. Not a substitute for reading the actual books.

skills.name: crucial-conversations
skills.title: Crucial Conversations
skills.description: Use when asked how to handle a high-stakes, emotionally charged conversation — the CPR/CRIB/AMPP/WWWF frameworks from the "Crucial Conversations" book — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/crucial-conversations, distinct from general team communication norms (see ways-of-working).

skills.name: deliberate-practice
skills.title: Deliberate Practice
skills.description: Use when asked to design, audit, or fix practice so it actually builds skill — a goal just past current ability, full concentration, immediate specific feedback, and repetition with correction — or when someone has practiced for a long time without improving. Distinct from [[getting-feedback]] (how to receive feedback well), [[always-improving]] (the general habit of continuous improvement), and [[smart-criteria]] (how to word a goal), each of which it draws on.

skills.name: getting-feedback
skills.title: Getting Feedback
skills.description: Use when asked how to seek out or receive feedback well — actively soliciting it, listening without immediately defending, separating the signal from delivery, and deciding what to act on — as the complement to giving-feedback.

skills.name: giving-feedback
skills.title: Giving Feedback
skills.description: Use when asked to give feedback effectively — being specific and behavior-focused, timing, balancing positive and constructive feedback, and delivering it in a way the recipient can actually act on — as the complement to getting-feedback.

skills.name: inclusive-language
skills.title: Inclusive Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write or review text for inclusive language — gender-neutral role names and pronouns, disability-respectful phrasing, or non-gendered technology/business terminology (master/slave, whitelist/blacklist alternatives) — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/inclusive-language. Adapt to the specific audience and context rather than applying mechanically.

skills.name: systems-thinking
skills.title: Systems Thinking
skills.description: Use when asked to analyze a problem as an interconnected system — feedback loops, stocks and flows, leverage points — rather than a chain of independent parts, before reaching for a specific method that assumes linear cause-and-effect (as distinct from applying vanguard-method's service-specific application, or causal-analysis-based-on-system-theory's accident-investigation application, of the same underlying discipline).

skills.name: medical-advance-directive
skills.title: Medical Advance Directive
skills.description: Use when asked to draft, review, or explain an advance directive (living will) or health care proxy designation — a document stating future medical treatment wishes or naming a decision-maker for when a person can't communicate them — for general educational and structural guidance only, not medical or legal advice; requirements vary by jurisdiction — always follow institutional policy and consult the treating clinician and, where legal validity matters, a qualified lawyer.

skills.name: medical-do-not-resuscitate-order
skills.title: Medical Do Not Resuscitate Order
skills.description: Use when asked to document, explain, or structure a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order — a clinician-written medical order instructing that CPR not be attempted if a patient's heart or breathing stops — for general educational and structural guidance only, not medical or legal advice; requirements vary by jurisdiction — always follow institutional policy and consult the treating clinician and, where legal validity matters, a qualified lawyer.

skills.name: medical-informed-consent
skills.title: Medical Informed Consent
skills.description: Use when asked to document, explain, or structure the informed consent process for a treatment or procedure — the conversation and record confirming a patient understands and voluntarily agrees before it happens — for general educational and structural guidance only, not medical or legal advice; requirements vary by jurisdiction — always follow institutional policy and consult the treating clinician and, where legal validity matters, a qualified lawyer.

skills.name: brainstorming
skills.title: Brainstorming
skills.description: Use when asked to run a brainstorming session well — quantity-over-quality, non-judgmental atmosphere, timeboxing, and capture technique — the foundational technique within the broader creative-thinking toolkit (see creative-thinking).

skills.name: creative-thinking
skills.title: Creative Thinking
skills.description: Use when asked which creative-thinking technique fits a situation — an umbrella overview of brainstorming, mind mapping, SCAMPER, random association, analogies, thinking hats, mindful observation, and storyboarding — as the technique-selection layer above ideation's general discipline.

skills.name: flowchart
skills.title: Flowchart
skills.description: Use when asked to draw a flowchart — start/end, process, decision, connector, and input/output symbols representing a process or workflow's sequence — as distinct from a mind map's radial, associative structure (see mind-map), which suits non-sequential idea structures rather than linear/branching process flow.

skills.name: futurespective
skills.title: Futurespective
skills.description: Use when asked to run a futurespective — a forward-looking group exercise imagining possible future scenarios to inform current decisions — as the forward-facing counterpart to a retrospective, drawing on scenario planning and SWOT analysis (see swot-analysis).

skills.name: ideation
skills.title: Ideation
skills.description: Use when asked to generate ideas or run a brainstorming session — divergent thinking, mind mapping, SCAMPER, and other idea-generation techniques — as the generative phase that precedes evaluation/selection, distinct from decision-making tools like decision-tree used afterward.

skills.name: mental-model
skills.title: Mental Model
skills.description: Use when asked to apply or explain a mental model — the cognitive frameworks people use to simplify, predict, and reason about a domain — as the general concept underlying more specific frameworks throughout this collection (SWOT, PDCA, OODA, and others are each a named mental model).

skills.name: mind-map
skills.title: Mind Map
skills.description: Use when asked to build a mind map — a central-idea-with-radiating-branches visual structure for brainstorming, note-taking, or organizing information — one specific technique within the broader ideation toolkit (see ideation).

skills.name: oblique-strategies
skills.title: Oblique Strategies
skills.description: Use when asked for a creative-block-breaking prompt, or to explain Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt's "Oblique Strategies" card deck — lateral-thinking prompts for getting unstuck on a creative or technical problem — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/oblique-strategies.

skills.name: scamper
skills.title: Scamper
skills.description: Use when asked to apply SCAMPER — a seven-prompt checklist (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse) for generating variations on an existing idea — one specific structured technique within the broader creative-thinking toolkit (see creative-thinking).

skills.name: thinking-hats
skills.title: Thinking Hats
skills.description: Use when asked to apply the Six Thinking Hats technique — deliberately switching between factual, emotional, critical, optimistic, creative, and process-level thinking modes — one specific structured technique within the broader creative-thinking toolkit (see creative-thinking).

skills.name: adversary
skills.title: Adversary
skills.description: Use when asked to role-play the person or organization that opposes the user, their plan, or their success — a competitor, rival, or someone who benefits from their failure — and lay out exactly where and how they would compete, undermine, or thwart it, including moves the user would not see coming. Distinct from a [[premortem]] (imagines the plan has failed and explains why, with no opposing agent), from [[competitor-analysis]] (describes competitors as they are, not how a motivated one would attack), and from the full [[foresight]] sequence, where it is the fourth stage.

skills.name: decision-analysis
skills.title: Decision Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to carry out a structured, end-to-end analysis of a significant decision under uncertainty — frame the decision, define objectives and alternatives, model uncertainties and values, evaluate, run sensitivity analysis, and decide whether more information is worth buying — as distinct from a single technique such as a [[decision-tree]], [[expected-value-analysis]], or [[weighted-decision-matrix]], which it may use, and from [[game-theory]] (where other parties choose strategically).

skills.name: decision-journal
skills.title: Decision Journal
skills.description: Use when asked to record an important decision at the moment it is made — the situation, options, reasoning, expectations with probabilities, and mental state — and to review it later so the quality of the decision can be judged separately from its outcome and judgment can improve over time; distinct from [[architecture-decision-record]] and [[decision-records]] (shared, formal records of choices for an organization), general [[journaling]], and a [[postmortem]] (analysis of a failure after it happened).

skills.name: decision-tree
skills.title: Decision Tree
skills.description: Use when asked to build a decision tree — a branching structure of decisions and their outcomes, for classification, prediction, or evaluating scenarios — as one structured evaluation tool, distinct from the generative, judgment-free phase of ideation (see ideation) that typically precedes it.

skills.name: expected-value-analysis
skills.title: Expected Value Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to compare uncertain options by estimating the possible outcomes of each, their probabilities, and their payoffs, then computing the probability-weighted average (expected value) while also examining the spread, worst case, and sensitivity to the estimates — as distinct from a [[decision-tree]] (sequential decisions, though it uses expected value at its nodes), a [[weighted-decision-matrix]] (multiple criteria, no probabilities), and [[bayes-theorem-analysis]] (updating probabilities from evidence).

skills.name: foresight
skills.title: Foresight
skills.description: Use when asked to stress-test a plan end to end before executing it — a five-stage sequence of [[premortem]] (autopsy of the failed plan), verdict (most likely vs. most dangerous failure and the biggest hidden assumption), rebuild (a plan with every failure closed off plus a pre-launch checklist with walk-away results), [[adversary]] (the opponent's attack on the rebuilt plan), and [[tripwire]] (a measurable signal and check day per failure). Use for launches, hires, investments, career moves, and projects not yet started; not for a single stage alone, for an incident already happened ([[postmortem]]), or for a plan too early to have a timeline and success definition.

skills.name: game-theory
skills.title: Game Theory
skills.description: Use when asked to analyze a decision whose outcome depends on what other rational parties will choose — identify the players, their options, payoffs, and information, then find dominant strategies, equilibria, and ways to change the game (commitments, repetition, side payments) — as distinct from [[expected-value-analysis]] (one decision-maker against uncertain nature), a [[decision-tree]] (no strategic opponent), and [[second-order-thinking]] (general downstream consequences without formal payoffs).

skills.name: ooda-loop
skills.title: OODA Loop
skills.description: Use when asked to explain or apply the OODA loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) — John Boyd's decision-cycle theory — for business strategy or competitive situations, or to compare it against PDCA/DMAIC — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/ooda-loop.

skills.name: premortem
skills.title: Premortem
skills.description: Use when asked to stress-test a plan before committing to it by assuming it has already failed and writing the autopsy — a prospective, failure-first analysis of a plan's likeliest causes of death, the assumptions behind them, and the first warning sign of each — as distinct from a [[postmortem]] (analyzing a failure that already happened), a generic risk list ([[risk-register]]), and the full five-stage [[foresight]] sequence, of which the premortem is the first stage.

skills.name: prospect-theory
skills.title: Prospect Theory
skills.description: Use when asked to understand or predict how people actually judge risky choices — evaluating outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, feeling losses more than equal gains, overweighting small probabilities, and being swayed by framing — in order to debug one's own decisions, design offers, or explain surprising behavior; distinct from [[expected-value-analysis]] (the rational benchmark it departs from), [[game-theory]] (strategic interaction), and [[decision-analysis]] (the structured process it can inform).

skills.name: regret-minimization
skills.title: Regret Minimization
skills.description: Use when asked to decide a personal or career-scale choice where numbers do not settle it, by imagining oneself at a distant future point (for example age 80, or ten years on) and asking which option would be regretted least — covering regret of action versus inaction, regret of omission, and what the decision reveals about values — as distinct from a [[weighted-decision-matrix]] (quantified criteria), [[premortem]] (assuming a plan failed), and general [[journaling]].

skills.name: second-order-thinking
skills.title: Second Order Thinking
skills.description: Use when asked to look past the immediate result of a decision to its downstream consequences — the reactions, feedback loops, and side effects that follow the first effect, and then what follows those — to catch decisions that look good now and backfire later; distinct from [[systems-thinking]] (the wider discipline of modeling interacting parts), a [[premortem]] (assumes failure and asks why), and [[strategic-flywheel-effects]] (a specific reinforcing loop).

skills.name: tripwire
skills.title: Tripwire
skills.description: Use when asked to turn failure modes, dangers, or risks into tripwires — for each one, a single measurable signal that shows it is starting to happen, a threshold, and an exact time or cadence to check — rather than vague "keep an eye on it" monitoring. Distinct from [[key-risk-indicators]] (the general practice of risk metrics across an organization), a [[risk-register]] (which records the risk but not necessarily its trigger), and the full [[foresight]] sequence, where it is the fifth stage.

skills.name: two-way-door-decisions
skills.title: Two Way Door Decisions
skills.description: Use when asked to decide how much deliberation, evidence, and approval a decision deserves by classifying it as reversible (a two-way door, decide fast and adjust) or hard to reverse (a one-way door, slow down and verify), and to find ways to turn one-way doors into two-way ones — as distinct from a [[weighted-decision-matrix]] (choosing among options), a [[premortem]] (stress-testing a chosen plan), and [[architecture-decision-record]] (documenting a decision made).

skills.name: weighted-decision-matrix
skills.title: Weighted Decision Matrix
skills.description: Use when asked to choose among several options against multiple criteria that matter by different amounts — score each option on each criterion, weight the criteria, total the results, and test how sensitive the winner is to the weights — as distinct from a [[decision-tree]] (sequential choices under uncertainty), [[expected-value-analysis]] (a single quantity under probabilities), and a plain pros-and-cons list (unweighted, unstructured).

skills.name: enterprise-architecture
skills.title: Enterprise Architecture
skills.description: Use when asked to align an organization's business processes, information systems, and technology infrastructure at the whole-enterprise level — business/information/technology/application architecture — as distinct from a single system's software-architecture.

skills.name: enterprise-change-management
skills.title: Enterprise Change Management
skills.description: Use when asked to plan or run change management for a large organizational change (merger, reorganization, major technology rollout) — planning/implementation/evaluation stages, stakeholder engagement, resistance — as ECM, distinct from the specific change-improvement techniques in dmaic, kaizen, and adkar.

skills.name: enterprise-portfolio-project-management
skills.title: Enterprise Portfolio Project Management
skills.description: Use when asked to manage an organization's whole project portfolio strategically — identification/prioritization, resource allocation, portfolio-level risk management, performance tracking — as EPPM, a large-organization-scale application of portfolio-management's concepts.

skills.name: enterprise-resource-planning
skills.title: Enterprise Resource Planning
skills.description: Use when asked about ERP systems — integrated software managing finance, accounting, HR, supply chain, and CRM in one centralized platform — for understanding what an ERP system does, its benefits, and implementation considerations.

skills.name: break-even-analysis
skills.title: Break-Even Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to find the break-even point — the sales volume or revenue at which total costs equal total revenue — to sanity-check a price, a new product, or an initiative before committing, as distinct from [[unit-economics]], which asks whether a single customer is profitable rather than when the whole initiative stops losing money.

skills.name: budget-forecasting
skills.title: Budget Forecasting
skills.description: Use when asked to build or maintain a budget forecast — the ongoing, continuously updated projection of future income and expenses against actuals — as distinct from a budget itself, which is a fixed plan or target set for a period rather than a live projection.

skills.name: cap-table
skills.title: Cap Table
skills.description: Use when asked to build, read, or explain a capitalization table — who owns what percentage of a company across founders, employees, and investors, and how funding rounds dilute that ownership — as distinct from a [[business-model-canvas]], which describes how the business operates rather than who owns it.

skills.name: personal-budget
skills.title: Personal Budget
skills.description: Use when asked to build or review a personal or household budget — a plan for an individual's or family's own income and spending — distinct from [[budget-forecasting]], which projects revenue and costs for an organization rather than a person or household.

skills.name: roi-analysis
skills.title: ROI Analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to calculate or compare the return on investment (ROI) of a decision or initiative — net benefit relative to cost — as distinct from a [[budget-forecasting]] projection, which tracks overall income and expense over time rather than evaluating one specific investment decision.

skills.name: unit-economics
skills.title: Unit Economics
skills.description: Use when asked to analyze or explain the profitability of a business at the level of one customer or unit — lifetime value, acquisition cost, contribution margin — as distinct from a full financial model or [[roi-analysis]] of a single project or investment.

skills.name: balance-and-stability-fitness
skills.title: Balance and Stability Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on balance and stability training — proprioception, single-leg work, and why this matters across ages and fitness levels.

skills.name: bodyweight-fitness
skills.title: Bodyweight Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on bodyweight training (calisthenics) — progressions, common movement patterns, and building strength without equipment.

skills.name: cardio-fitness
skills.title: Cardio Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on cardiovascular (cardio) fitness training — heart-rate zones, steady-state vs. interval training, and building an aerobic base.

skills.name: core-fitness
skills.title: Core Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on core training — training beyond visible abs, anti-extension/rotation work, and how core strength supports other fitness goals.

skills.name: crossfit-fitness
skills.title: Crossfit Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on CrossFit-style training — constantly varied, high-intensity functional movement, scaling for beginners, and the role of coaching.

skills.name: endurance-fitness
skills.title: Endurance Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on endurance training — building toward sustained, longer-duration performance (running, cycling, swimming, or multi-sport events).

skills.name: flexibility-and-mobility-fitness
skills.title: Flexibility and Mobility Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on flexibility and mobility training — static vs. dynamic stretching, when to use each, and building a mobility routine.

skills.name: functional-fitness
skills.title: Functional Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on functional fitness training — movements that mimic real-world activities, multi-joint patterns, and training for everyday capability rather than isolated muscle size.

skills.name: group-fitness
skills.title: Group Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on group fitness classes — choosing a class type, getting the most from group instruction, and how it compares to solo training.

skills.name: hiit-fitness
skills.title: Hiit Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on HIIT (high-intensity interval training) — structuring work/rest intervals, who it's suited for, and recovery demands.

skills.name: home-gym-fitness
skills.title: Home Gym Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on building a home gym — prioritizing equipment, space and budget trade-offs, and getting real training value without a commercial gym.

skills.name: injury-prevention-fitness
skills.title: Injury Prevention Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on injury prevention in fitness training — warm-up, gradual progression, and recognizing early warning signs before they become serious injuries.

skills.name: personal-training-fitness
skills.title: Personal Training Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on working with a personal trainer — what to look for in a trainer, how to set goals together, and getting the most value from sessions.

skills.name: pilates
skills.title: Pilates
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on Pilates as a fitness discipline — core-centered control, breath coordination, and mat vs. equipment-based practice.

skills.name: powerlifting
skills.title: Powerlifting
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on powerlifting — the squat, bench press, and deadlift as a competitive or training discipline, including programming and form fundamentals.

skills.name: prenatal-fitness
skills.title: Prenatal Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on prenatal fitness — safe exercise during pregnancy, exercises and positions to modify or avoid, and the importance of medical guidance.

skills.name: progress-tracking-fitness
skills.title: Progress Tracking Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on tracking fitness progress — what metrics to track for different goals, and avoiding over-reliance on any single number.

skills.name: recovery-and-rest-fitness
skills.title: Recovery and Rest Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on fitness recovery and rest — sleep, rest days, and recognizing overtraining — the often-neglected counterpart to training itself.

skills.name: senior-fitness
skills.title: Senior Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on fitness training for older adults — balancing strength, balance, and cardiovascular training with safety and mobility considerations.

skills.name: sports-nutrition-fitness
skills.title: Sports Nutrition Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on sports/fitness nutrition — protein needs, pre/post-workout fueling, and hydration for training and performance.

skills.name: strength-training-fitness
skills.title: Strength Training Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on strength training — progressive overload, compound lifts, and program structure for someone building a resistance-training routine.

skills.name: warm-up-and-cool-down-fitness
skills.title: Warm Up and Cool Down Fitness
skills.description: Use when asked for guidance on structuring a workout warm-up and cool-down — what each should include and why both matter for performance and recovery.

skills.name: government-constituent-casework
skills.title: Government Constituent Casework
skills.description: Use when asked to set up or run constituent casework — an elected official's office helping an individual constituent resolve a problem with a government agency (a US member of Congress's district office, a UK MP's constituency office, a local councillor's casework) — distinct from [[government-ombudsman-complaint-investigation]], which investigates whether an agency itself acted unfairly rather than helping someone navigate it.

skills.name: government-ombudsman-complaint-investigation
skills.title: Government Ombudsman Complaint Investigation
skills.description: Use when asked to conduct or write up an ombudsman investigation into a complaint that a government body acted unfairly or made a maladministration error — distinct from a legal appeal, since an ombudsman typically examines fairness and process rather than the legal merits of a decision, and usually can only recommend a remedy rather than compel one (details vary by jurisdiction and specific ombudsman scheme).

skills.name: government-public-hearing
skills.title: Government Public Hearing
skills.description: Use when asked to plan, notice, or run a public hearing — a formal public meeting where a government body takes testimony or comment on a specific matter (a zoning decision, a proposed budget, a piece of legislation) before deciding — distinct from [[government-legislative-testimony]], which is testimony to a legislative committee specifically and typically without general public sign-up.

skills.name: government-contract-proposal
skills.title: Government Contract Proposal
skills.description: Use when asked to write or review a bid responding to a government solicitation for goods or services — distinct from a commercial [[sales-proposal]], since government procurement typically carries formal compliance requirements, published evaluation criteria, and sometimes set-aside programs for specific categories of bidder, all of which vary significantly by country and level of government.

skills.name: government-emergency-management-plan
skills.title: Government Emergency Management Plan
skills.description: Use when asked to write or review a government emergency management plan — a jurisdiction's plan for coordinating multi-agency response to a civil emergency such as a natural disaster, public health emergency, or major infrastructure failure — distinct from a single organization's [[business-continuity-plan]], which is one organization's internal continuity rather than coordination across multiple agencies and the public.

skills.name: government-open-data-publication
skills.title: Government Open Data Publication
skills.description: Use when asked to plan or review a government open data publication — a government body proactively publishing datasets for public and reuse, on an ongoing basis and with no request required — distinct from [[freedom-of-information-request]], which is a reactive response to one individual's specific request rather than proactive, ongoing publication.

skills.name: government-performance-report
skills.title: Government Performance Report
skills.description: Use when asked to write or review a government performance report — a government body's disclosure of its own performance against stated goals or metrics, to a legislature and/or the public — distinct from [[sustainability-report]], which is specifically ESG/environmental-social-governance disclosure rather than broader mission-accountability reporting.

skills.name: government-public-budget-appropriation
skills.title: Government Public Budget Appropriation
skills.description: Use when asked to draft, review, or explain a public budget appropriation — the formal government process of allocating public funds to specific purposes for a budget period — distinct from organizational [[budget-forecasting]], since this is a legislative or political appropriations process where a legislature or council formally authorizes spending, not an internal projection exercise.

skills.name: government-public-records-management
skills.title: Government Public Records Management
skills.description: Use when asked to advise on or design a government public records management process — how a government body manages the lifecycle of its official records, from creation through retention to disposal or archiving, under whatever public-records retention law applies — noting, in the same vein as [[freedom-of-information-request]]'s treatment of FOI law, that retention schedules and requirements vary significantly by country and agency.

skills.name: government-security-clearance-application
skills.title: Government Security Clearance Application
skills.description: Use when asked to advise on applying for or maintaining a government security clearance for a position requiring access to classified or sensitive information — noting that clearance levels, required forms, adjudication criteria, and reciprocity between agencies vary significantly by country and are governed by specific national security law, so this is general structural guidance, not a substitute for the specific agency's own instructions.

skills.name: care-plan
skills.title: Care Plan
skills.description: Use when asked to organize a care plan for an aging or ill family member — a checklist covering legal, medical, financial, and long-term care areas — grounded in joelparkerhenderson/care-plan. This is general organizational guidance, not medical, legal, or financial advice for a specific person's situation.

skills.name: first-aid
skills.title: First Aid
skills.description: Use when asked for general first-aid knowledge — the primary survey (DRABC/DRSABC), treating bleeding, burns, choking, or shock, or recovery position technique. This is general educational information, not medical advice for a specific person's condition — always direct a real emergency to local emergency services and in-person trained care.

skills.name: health-care
skills.title: Health Care
skills.description: Use when asked general questions about how health care systems and terminology work — care tiers (primary/secondary/tertiary), health insurance concepts, patient rights, or navigating a health system. This is general educational information about how health care works, not medical advice, diagnosis, or guidance for a specific person's condition — for symptoms or an actual emergency, see urgent-emergency-care.

skills.name: urgent-emergency-care
skills.title: Urgent Emergency Care
skills.description: Use when asked how to recognize a medical emergency, decide between emergency care and urgent/primary care, or what to say when calling emergency services. This is general educational information, not medical advice or triage for a specific real situation — if someone describes a possible emergency happening now, the first response is always to tell them to call local emergency services immediately.

skills.name: allergy-care
skills.title: Allergy Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about allergy care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: alzheimers-disease-care
skills.title: Alzheimers Disease Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about Alzheimer's disease care — common symptoms, general self-care and caregiving measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: anxiety-care
skills.title: Anxiety Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about anxiety care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: arthritis-care
skills.title: Arthritis Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about arthritis care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: attention-deficit-care
skills.title: Attention Deficit Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about ADHD (attention deficit) care — common symptoms, general self-care and management measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: autism-care
skills.title: Autism Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about autism care and support — common characteristics, general support measures, and when to seek professional guidance — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or relevant specialist.

skills.name: bipolar-care
skills.title: Bipolar Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about bipolar disorder care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or mental health professional.

skills.name: cancer-care
skills.title: Cancer Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about cancer care — common symptoms, general self-care during treatment, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: cold-sore-care
skills.title: Cold Sore Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about cold sore (oral herpes) care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: concussion-care
skills.title: Concussion Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about concussion care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek urgent medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: croup-care
skills.title: Croup Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about croup care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: dehydration-care
skills.title: Dehydration Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about dehydration care — common symptoms, general self-care measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: dementia-care
skills.title: Dementia Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about dementia care — common symptoms, general self-care and caregiving measures, and when to seek medical attention — for education only, not medical advice; always direct the reader to consult a doctor or health care professional.

skills.name: dental-care
skills.title: Dental Care
skills.description: Use when asked for general educational information about dental/oral health care — common issues, general self-care measures, and when to seek dental attention — for education only, not medical/dental advice; always direct the reader to consult a dentist or health care professional.

skills.name: arabic-language

skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in Arabic — a right-to-left abjad script that normally omits short vowels, root-and-pattern morphology, and a major gap between Modern Standard Arabic and regional spoken dialects; official across the Middle East and North Africa with hundreds of millions of speakers.

skills.name: cymraeg-language
skills.title: Cymraeg Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in Cymraeg (Welsh) — a Celtic language with initial consonant mutations, digraphs treated as single alphabet letters, and grammatical gender — spoken mainly in Wales with official status alongside English.

skills.name: dutch-language
skills.title: Dutch Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in Dutch — the common/neuter gender system, verb-second word order in main clauses, the u/jij formal-informal distinction, and real vocabulary differences between Netherlandic and Flemish Dutch, official in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Suriname.

skills.name: french-language
skills.title: French Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in French — grammatical gender agreement, the vous/tu formal-informal and plural distinction, and liaison/elision conventions, official across France, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada, and many African countries.

skills.name: gaeilge-language
skills.title: Gaeilge Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in Gaeilge (Irish) — a Celtic language with initial mutations (lenition and eclipsis), the síneadh fada marking long vowels, and verb-subject-object word order — an official language of Ireland and of the EU, with a minority of first-language speakers.

skills.name: gaidhlig-language
skills.title: Gaidhlig Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in Gàidhlig (Scottish Gaelic) — a Celtic language with lenition-style initial mutations, the grave accent marking long vowels, verb-subject-object word order, and a vocative case — spoken mainly in the Scottish Highlands and Islands with official recognition in Scotland.

skills.name: german-language
skills.title: German Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in German (Deutsch) — a Germanic language with a four-case noun system, grammatical gender that must be memorized per noun, and long compound nouns — official in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, with real regional variation.

skills.name: hindi-language
skills.title: Hindi Language

skills.name: indonesian-language
skills.title: Indonesian Language

skills.name: italian-language
skills.title: Italian Language
skills.description: Use when asked to write, translate into, or check text in Italian — grammatical gender agreement, the tu/Lei formal-informal distinction (where Lei takes third-person verb forms), and a largely phonetic spelling system, official in Italy, Switzerland, San Marino, and Vatican City.
